title: Discounts, Coupons and Loyalty: Promotions Without Chaos
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/08-promotions-and-loyalty/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter. It is a contract, not a description: the places where the published chapter did not do what the spec asks are listed under open_questions and decision_log.

know: The parts of a promotion system: definitions with an order of evaluation and a stop rule, eligibility, the code ledger, evaluation in the cart, allocation to order lines.
Why gift cards, store credit and loyalty points are liabilities held in ledgers and not promotions.
believe: A promotion incident is a governance failure (a setting without an owner) before it is a software failure.
The allocated net line price, not the list price, is the price every later system must read.
can_do: Allocate an order-level discount to lines and compute the refund for one returned line.
Ask of any promotion setup which system computes the final discount, in what order, where stacking stops and who may change that.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture. The ecommerce manager who configures campaigns and the engineer who owns the order export benefit most: the chapter shows them the same promotion from the cart's side and from the invoice's side. Finance readers get the liability and breakage rules in plain words; product managers get the choices and the scale-stage judgement.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side, including typing a discount code and paying with a gift card.

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, what a system is, 'the shop platform' for the hosted product, Kestrel & Pine's systems, people and incidents in outline, the four scale stages, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation, Waypoint decisions W1 to W8, the failure-pattern names.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub / order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.
From the two chapters before this one: product information owned per attribute, and a price selected by one rule and frozen on the order.
does_not_know: Promotion, coupon code, automatic discount, eligibility, stacking, order of evaluation, stop rule, discount allocation, net line price.
Gift card, store credit and loyalty points as liabilities; breakage, material right, contract liability, deferred revenue.
Prior price, strike-through price, incrementality, holdout group.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an order with an order-level discount and one returned line, the reader computes the refund from the allocated net line price and says what had to be recorded at order time.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An order holds a €199 jacket and €36 of socks, with a 10% code on the whole order. The customer returns the jacket. Using only this chapter: how much is refunded, and what must have been recorded when the order was placed?
acceptance_criteria.expected: €179.10, not €199: the €23.50 discount is allocated to the lines in proportion (€19.90 to the jacket), and the net price per line is written to the order, where the returns tool, the invoice and the credit note read it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two discounts that combined against the business's intent, the reader names the missing owner of the combination rule and a test against the active promotions, before naming a new tool.
acceptance_criteria.probe: In a sale week a welcome code combined with an automatic 20% discount on the same carts, although nobody intended it. Using only this chapter: what was missing, and what would you do before the next campaign?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The rule that decides stacking lived in a platform setting that nobody owned or checked against the campaign plan. Give the combination settings one owner, write each campaign with its order of evaluation and stop rule in one calendar, and test the new campaign against every promotion already active. Governance first, not a new promotion engine.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say why a gift-card balance is not a discount and who must check it against what.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: why is a gift card not a promotion, and who has to check its balance against what, how often?
acceptance_criteria.expected: It is value the customer has paid for in advance, so the merchant owes it: a liability kept as a ledger with a balance. Finance reconciles the stored-value balances to a liability account every month.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: What a promotion is and what it touches; the parts of a promotion system and where the final discount is computed; how a discount reaches the invoice, the refund and the books; gift cards, store credit and points as ledgers; the choices by scale stage; dated examples and Kestrel & Pine's 2027 plan; how promotions fail. Evidence: the Black Friday Stacking Bug, a worked allocation on Eva's order, platform documentation, accounting standards and a company filing.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How do you offer discounts, coupons, bundles and loyalty rewards without breaking the price, the margin or the books?
thesis.claim: Promotions leave the price, the margin and the books intact when three things hold: each promotion, whether a discount, a coupon or a bundle, is a data record with a place in a declared order of evaluation and a rule that says where stacking (combining promotions on one order) stops; the final discount is computed once, in the cart, and written to the order allocated to its lines, so that invoices and refunds read the net price of each line; and gift cards, store credit and loyalty points are kept apart from promotions as ledgers of value the merchant owes its customers, reconciled every month to a liability account.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a promotion is a marketing setting a campaign manager switches on in the shop platform, that the discount shown on the product page is the discount, and that a gift card or a loyalty point is one more kind of discount.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's Black Friday Stacking Bug put two discounts on 2,860 orders and cost about €52,000, part of it refunded twice on returns. A merchant that accepts the claim gives the combination settings one owner, tests each campaign against the promotions already active, and makes its order export carry the net price per line.
thesis.how_why: Two promotions that are each valid combine unless a rule says where stacking stops; when that rule is a platform setting nobody owns, nobody checks it against a new campaign. The product page is rendered before the cart exists, so it can only estimate; the cart is the first place where all lines, codes and the customer are known. Invoices, tax, returns and partial refunds work line by line, so a discount left at order level is refunded at the wrong amount. A gift-card balance is money already received for goods not yet delivered, and a loyalty point is a reward the customer has already earned, so accounting standards record both as liabilities.

supporting_claims.claim: Two promotions that are each valid combine against the business's intent when the rule that decides stacking is a platform setting nobody owns or tests, so a promotion incident is a governance failure before it is a software failure.
A promotion is a data record: a type, conditions of eligibility, a usage record, and a place in a declared order of evaluation with a rule that says where stacking stops.

The final discount is computed once, in the cart, and written to the order allocated to its lines, because the product page can only estimate and because invoices, tax, returns and refunds work line by line.
Gift cards, store credit and loyalty points are value the merchant owes its customers, kept as ledgers apart from promotions and reconciled every month to a liability account.

How much promotion machinery a merchant needs depends on how many systems must agree on the result, so the platform's own promotions with clear ownership are enough until one promotion must be the same rule in two systems the platform does not control.
What the law, abuse and measurement ask of promotions arrives as requirements on recorded data: a price history, a usage record per customer identity and a record of what was offered.

role.contribution: Shows what may be subtracted from a selected price and how the result is fixed on the order, so that the price a later system reads is the one the customer paid.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene through pieces: the incident, then the vocabulary and the system that would have prevented it
choices, in-practice and when-it-goes-wrong: parallel options, parallel findings and parallel failures

flow.rationale: The incident comes first because it gives the reader three concrete faults to carry through the chapter. The vocabulary follows because the faults cannot be named exactly without it, and the system description follows the vocabulary because its five parts are described in those words. Stored value comes after the promotion system because it is defined by contrast with it: a reader who met the ledgers first would not yet know what they are being kept apart from. The choices and the scale stages need both halves, since the comparison of the four options has a row for allocation and a row for stored value; moved before the system description, it would compare options on criteria not yet explained. The public examples follow the choices because each names a record (a price history, a customer identity, the offers made) that the chosen arrangement must keep, and the 2027 plan closes them because it applies the governance rule the choices end on. The failures come last because each is the absence of something an earlier section established.

hook.content: A shopper uses a welcome code to buy a jacket and socks, then returns the jacket. How much should the merchant refund?

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone who has typed a discount code or spent a gift card knows promotions from the shopper's side, where the discount is simply a lower total.
bridge.to_topic: The refund question shows that the total is not enough: the discount has to be recorded per item, the combination of offers has to be decided by a rule, and a stored balance is a debt and not a discount.

thesis_statement.text: A promotion is a rule evaluated in one place, at cart time, in a declared order with a rule that says when stacking stops; the discount is not finished until it is allocated to lines; gift cards, store credit and points are money owed, kept as ledgers and reconciled to a liability account every month.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout, all three bullets; paragraphs p01 to p03 state the three parts in prose

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and paragraph p05

promises.promise: Start from Kestrel & Pine's Black Friday Stacking Bug.
Define a promotion and what it touches.
Describe the parts of a promotion system and where the final discount is computed, and follow a discount to the invoice, the refund and the books with a worked allocation on Eva's order.
Treat gift cards, store credit and points as ledgers of money owed.
Compare four ways to run promotions and say how each fits the scale stages.
Give dated examples and Kestrel & Pine's plan for Black Friday 2027.
List the ways promotions fail, with detection and recovery.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A shopper who used a welcome code on a jacket and socks returns the jacket, and the right refund depends on how the discount was shared across the items, so a promotion needs a recorded calculation that checkout, returns and finance all use.

evidence.what: A welcome code on a jacket and socks, then a return of the jacket; a returns system that reads the list price refunds more than the shopper paid.
evidence.shows: One ordinary return is enough to show that a discount has to be recorded per item.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Offers also interact before payment: two valid discounts can combine into a price the business never intended, so the promotion rules must say which combinations apply.

transition_in.carries_over: The discount whose share per item decides the refund.
transition_in.introduces: A second way a promotion goes wrong, before payment: two valid offers combining.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Gift cards and loyalty points are a different obligation from a discount: a balance the customer can still spend, which the merchant owes and must keep a record of.

transition_in.carries_over: Discounts and how they combine.
transition_in.introduces: Stored balances, which are owed to the customer and are not discounts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The previous chapter selected a price by rule and froze it on the order; this chapter covers what may be subtracted from that price at checkout, and Eva's order of 13 April 2027 already carries one promotion, free shipping over €75.

evidence.what: Eva's order at Kestrel & Pine on 13 April 2027: a €199 jacket and two €18 pairs of socks, €235 in total, no item discount, free shipping over €75.
evidence.shows: Even an order with no discount code passes through promotion evaluation.

transition_in.carries_over: Discounts and balances as things that must be recorded.
transition_in.introduces: The place of promotions in the order's journey, after the price is selected, and the one promotion on Eva's order.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter starts from Kestrel & Pine's Black Friday Stacking Bug, defines a promotion and what it touches, describes the parts of a promotion system and follows a discount to the invoice, the refund and the books, treats gift cards, store credit and points as ledgers, compares four ways to run promotions across the scale stages, and ends with dated examples, the 2027 plan and the ways promotions fail.

transition_in.carries_over: Where promotions sit in the order's journey.
transition_in.introduces: The order of the chapter's sections and the kinds of evidence it uses.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: The Black Friday Stacking Bug
sections.controlling_idea: In Black Friday week 2026 two valid promotions combined on 2,860 orders because of a setting nobody checked, and the cost of about €52,000 came from three separate faults: the stacking, the shipping threshold and the missing allocation.

advances_thesis.how: Shows in one incident that the stacking rule lived in an unowned setting, that the page and the cart computed the threshold differently, and that an unallocated order-level discount was refunded back.

flow.rationale: The promotions as configured, what the setting did to them, then the diagnosis: the reader needs the three promotions before the combination and the figures before the three faults are named.

transition_in.carries_over: Two valid discounts combining against intent, announced in the introduction.
transition_in.introduces: The incident at Kestrel & Pine in which that happened, with its figures.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For Black Friday week, 23–29 November 2026, Milan Petrov configured three promotions on the hosted shop platform: an automatic 20% off outerwear, the standing 10% welcome code and free shipping over €75.

evidence.what: The three promotions active in the week of 23–29 November 2026.
evidence.shows: Each promotion was valid on its own; the incident needed nothing unusual.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The welcome code was not meant to combine with the outerwear discount, but a combination setting the agency had switched on in October still allowed both and nobody checked it against the campaign plan; the week cost about €52,000 in three ways: two discounts on 2,860 orders, shipping charged on 1,140 orders after the page had promised it free, and 190 returns refunded too much.

evidence.what: 31,000 online orders in the week; 2,860 with both discounts; Ridgewalker €199 → €159.20 → €143.28; about €43,000 margin beyond plan; 1,140 orders charged €4.95 shipping after the page promised it free, about €5,600 refunded; 190 returns over-refunded, about €3,000; total about €52,000.
evidence.shows: The cost has three parts, each from a different fault, and each row is a figure the later sections explain.

transition_in.carries_over: The three promotions as configured.
transition_in.introduces: The intent that two of them should not combine, the setting that let them, and what the week cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three things went wrong, and the chapter returns to each: the stacking rule lived in a setting and not in the campaign, the free-shipping threshold was evaluated on different subtotals by the page and the cart, and the order-level discount was never allocated to the lines.

evidence.what: Figure 1: the jacket price falling from €199 to €159.20 to €143.28 because a combine switch was left on.
evidence.shows: The first of the three faults in one picture: the second discount applied on top of the first.

transition_in.carries_over: The three costs of the week: double discounts, shipping charged against the page's promise, over-refunded returns.
transition_in.introduces: The fault behind each, and the conclusion that a price nobody can reconstruct from the rules has no owner.

sections.heading: What a Promotion Is, and What It Touches
sections.controlling_idea: A promotion is a rule that lowers the price under stated conditions; it comes in seven shapes, each of which touches the price, the margin and the books, and stored value is not one of them.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the vocabulary (promotion, code, eligibility, stacking, allocation) in which the thesis is stated and sets stored value apart from the start.

flow.rationale: The definition, then its seven types, then what all the types have in common, then what is excluded: the exclusion makes sense only once the reader knows what a promotion is. Paid membership was cut after failing in four placements.

transition_in.carries_over: The three faults of the Stacking Bug: stacking, evaluation and allocation.
transition_in.introduces: Plain definitions of those words and of the kinds of promotion.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A promotion is a rule that lowers the price a customer pays under stated conditions, and five words describe it: coupon code, automatic discount, eligibility, stacking and discount allocation.

evidence.what: Figure 2: an eligibility rule card above four panels (coupon code, automatic, stacking, allocation).
evidence.shows: The five words in one picture, each tied to what it does to a price.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every platform supports the same seven types of promotion, and each type needs different facts to compute and changes a different part of the order.

evidence.what: Seven promotion types (percentage off, fixed amount off, order discount, buy X get Y, tiered, free shipping, bundle) with an example, what each needs to compute and what it changes.
evidence.shows: Product discounts change a line; order discounts change the total and must be allocated to lines.

evidence.what: Figure 3: seven tiles, one per promotion type.
evidence.shows: The seven types at a glance, grouped by whether they change a line, the total or the shipping.

transition_in.carries_over: The definition of a promotion.
transition_in.introduces: The seven types and what each needs and changes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every type touches three things the business cares about: the price the customer sees, the margin, and the books.

evidence.what: The Ridgewalker at €143.28 still cleared its €58 landed cost but gave up about a sixth of its planned Black Friday unit margin.
evidence.shows: Margin is lost without any single promotion being wrong.

evidence.what: Figure 4: one discount tag with arrows to a price tag, a margin bar and an invoice with a ledger.
evidence.shows: One discount reaches three places, which are the three things the chapter's question asks to keep intact.

transition_in.carries_over: The seven types and what each changes.
transition_in.introduces: The three things all of them touch: price, margin and books.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Gift cards, store credit and loyalty points look like promotions and are not: they are value the merchant owes, kept as ledgers, and get their own section.

transition_in.carries_over: What a promotion is and touches.
transition_in.introduces: The instruments that look like promotions and are money owed.

sections.heading: How the Pieces Fit Together
sections.controlling_idea: A promotion system has five parts arranged around one decision: the final discount is computed once, in the cart, and written to the order allocated per line, where the invoice, the credit note and the ledger read it.

advances_thesis.how: Carries the first two clauses of the thesis: promotions as data with a declared order and stop rule, and the discount computed once and allocated to lines, shown on Eva's order.

flow.rationale: The five parts in the order a discount passes through them, then the discount's path after the order with one worked case. The worked allocation and the refund close the section, and the stored-value section opens by contrasting money paid back with money owed before any order. The table of six moments was cut (it failed in both positions tried); its one distinction, that only code and stored-value redemption must be strongly consistent, is a sentence of the code ledger.

transition_in.carries_over: The vocabulary of promotions, the three things a promotion touches and what is not a promotion.
transition_in.introduces: The parts of the system that evaluates promotions, and the path of a discount from the cart to the books.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A promotion system has five parts, whatever product provides them, arranged around one decision: the final discount is computed once, in the cart, and written to the order with its allocation.

evidence.what: Figure 5: the product page shows an estimate; the promotion engine computes the final discount at cart time and writes it to the order per line, read by invoice, refund and analytics.
evidence.shows: Where each of the five parts sits and which of them the later systems read.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Promotion definitions: each promotion is a record with a position in the order of evaluation, and three vendors document the same shape, a declared order and a stop rule.

evidence.what: Shopify evaluates product, then order, then shipping discounts (the order that took the Stacking Bug's jacket from €199 to €159.20 to €143.28); commercetools gives each cart discount a sortOrder, a stacking mode and discount groups; Adobe Commerce has rule priority and 'Discard subsequent rules'.
evidence.shows: Three independent products arrive at promotions as data with a declared order and a stop rule.
evidence.source: Shopify Help Center, commercetools docs, Adobe Experience League (accessed November 2026)

transition_in.carries_over: The five parts.
transition_in.introduces: The first part, the definition record, and how three vendors order and stop evaluation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Eligibility and identity: conditions such as 'first order' need to know who the customer is, and a check on the e-mail address alone treats one person with two addresses as two first-time customers.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine's welcome code checked 'first order' by e-mail address.
evidence.shows: Eligibility is only as good as the customer identity behind it.

transition_in.carries_over: The definition record and its conditions.
transition_in.introduces: The second part: deciding who qualifies, which depends on customer identity.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The code ledger: every code has a usage record that must be strongly consistent at redemption, so that two checkouts cannot both take the last use; redemption reads the live record while most of the rest can be a cached copy.

evidence.what: Adobe generates single-use codes in batches with usage caps.
evidence.shows: A platform treats capped single-use codes as the basic defense against code sharing.

evidence.what: Code redemption reads the live record; the product page's estimate, publication and analytics can be cached copies with a known delay.
evidence.shows: Strong consistency is needed in two places, not everywhere.

transition_in.carries_over: Eligibility per customer.
transition_in.introduces: The third part: the record of how often a code has been used.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Evaluation in the cart: the engine applies the promotions in order to the cart's lines and stops where the stop rule says, and because some conditions are known only at checkout, the product page can show only an estimate.

evidence.what: Adobe: conditions on the shipping or payment method 'are met only in checkout after the specific shipping/payment methods are selected'.
evidence.shows: A vendor states that some conditions cannot be evaluated before checkout, which is why the page estimates.

transition_in.carries_over: Definitions, eligibility and codes, the inputs.
transition_in.introduces: The fourth part: the evaluation itself, and why it can be final only in the cart.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Allocation and events: the last part writes the result where later systems read it, as a net price on each order line and as an event for each promotion applied, redeemed or offered.

evidence.what: commercetools distributes an absolute cart discount proportionately, evenly or individually across the lines.
evidence.shows: Allocation is a documented choice of the engine, not an afterthought.

transition_in.carries_over: The discount the cart computed.
transition_in.introduces: The fifth part: writing that discount to the order per line and emitting events.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A discount leaves the order in three documents, the invoice, the credit note and the general ledger, and each reads the net price per line, which makes allocation a tax matter as well.

evidence.what: An order-level discount across a jacket at 21% VAT and a hypothetical printed trail guide at 9% must be allocated before the tax can be right.
evidence.shows: Without allocation the VAT per line cannot be computed.

transition_in.carries_over: The net price written to each order line by the fifth part.
transition_in.introduces: The three documents that read it after the order: invoice, credit note and ledger.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On Eva's order of €235, a hypothetical 10% code is allocated in proportion to the list prices: €19.90 to the jacket and €3.60 to the socks.

evidence.what: Jacket €199.00, 84.7% of €235, discount €19.90, net €179.10; socks €36.00, 15.3%, discount €3.60, net €32.40; total discount €23.50, net €211.50. The code is hypothetical.
evidence.shows: The discount is split by each line's share of the order, and every line ends with a net price.

transition_in.carries_over: Allocation as the step the three documents depend on.
transition_in.introduces: The calculation on Eva's order.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: When Eva returns the jacket the refund is €179.10, not €199, and the 190 over-refunded Black Friday returns were this calculation skipped.

evidence.what: The returns portal read €159.20 because the order-level 10% had not been written to the lines, and gave back €15.92 per jacket that the customer had never paid.
evidence.shows: The over-refund is exactly the unallocated share of the discount.

evidence.what: Figure 6: a returns counter refunding €159.20 for a jacket paid at €143.28.
evidence.shows: The Boomerang pattern in one picture: the discount given a second time on the return.

transition_in.carries_over: The net line prices on Eva's order.
transition_in.introduces: The refund that follows from them, and the Stacking Bug's over-refunds as the same step missing.

sections.heading: Gift Cards, Store Credit and Points: Ledgers, Not Promotions
sections.controlling_idea: Gift cards, store credit and loyalty points are liabilities with settled accounting rules, so each is kept as a ledger whose balances finance reconciles to a liability account every month.

advances_thesis.how: Carries the third clause of the thesis: stored value is money owed, with its own records and its own monthly check.

flow.rationale: What the instruments are, the rules that make them liabilities, a filing that applies them, the design rules, then Kestrel & Pine's position: the design rules cannot be argued before the accounting that forces them. The sourcing note moved to the Sources section and paid membership to 'What a Promotion Is' in round 2, after both readers lost the argument at each.

transition_in.carries_over: The refund that gives back what was paid for a line.
transition_in.introduces: Value the merchant owes before any order: gift cards, store credit and points are balances, not rules.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A gift card is value paid in advance, store credit is value the merchant granted and loyalty points are value the customer earned, and all three are a liability on the balance sheet until redeemed or expired.

evidence.what: Figure 7: issuance, redemption, expiry and breakage changing a balance per instrument in the commerce platform, with the sum agreeing with the liability account in finance.
evidence.shows: Stored value is a ledger with two holders, the platform for the balance and finance for the liability.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For the three instruments the accounting is settled and drives the data model: under IFRS 15 and ASC 606 a gift-card sale is a liability and not revenue, the part never redeemed (breakage) is estimated, and points that give a material right defer revenue.

transition_in.carries_over: The three instruments as liabilities.
transition_in.introduces: The accounting standards that say so and what they require to be recorded.

evidence.what: IFRS 15 and ASC 606: a gift-card sale is a contract liability; breakage is estimated and recognized 'in proportion to the pattern of exercised rights'; PwC's revenue guide adds that breakage not expected is recognized only when redemption becomes remote, and that amounts due under unclaimed-property law are a liability, not revenue; material rights defer revenue.
evidence.shows: The accounting rules decide what the ledger must record.
evidence.source: PwC Viewpoint, Revenue guide 7.4; IFRS Foundation IFRS 15 page; IFRScommunity summary of B44-B47

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Starbucks' FY2025 annual report shows the same obligation at scale: a stored value card and loyalty liability of $1,751.7 million and $200.4 million of breakage recognized in the year.

evidence.what: Stored value card and loyalty liability $1,751.7 million; breakage recognized in company-operated stores $200.4 million; Stars deferred 'as each Star is earned' and expiring 'after six to twelve months, depending on the market'.
evidence.shows: A public filing records stored value as deferred revenue and estimates breakage; the obligation has the same shape for a merchant with €200,000 outstanding.
evidence.source: Starbucks Form 10-K, fiscal year ended 28 September 2025

transition_in.carries_over: The rules for liabilities and breakage.
transition_in.introduces: One company's filing that applies them, with amounts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four design rules follow: every instrument is a ledger, expiry belongs to the issuance, redemption is idempotent, and the platform's balances are reconciled to finance's liability account every month.

evidence.what: Shopify: 'Store credit expiration is set per issuance'.
evidence.shows: A platform models expiry the way the rule says.

transition_in.carries_over: The accounting rules and their scale.
transition_in.introduces: The four design rules they lead to.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's gift cards live in two separate pools, about €186,000 online and €41,000 in stores at 31 December 2026, which neither channel can redeem for the other and which finance reconciles each month from two exports.

evidence.what: Outstanding balances at 31 December 2026: about €186,000 online and €41,000 in stores; Sanne de Wit reconciles two exports to the liability account monthly.
evidence.shows: The monthly reconciliation exists, and the two pools are the price of two systems.

transition_in.carries_over: The design rules for stored value.
transition_in.introduces: How Kestrel & Pine's stored value stood at the end of 2026.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine deferred an online loyalty program until it can recognize the same customer across channels, and left a shared balance service to the 2028 store-system evaluation.

evidence.what: Stores keep a loyalty list; the online shop has none; a shared balance service is to be considered under decision W4.
evidence.shows: A points balance in an account the redemption system cannot identify would be a liability nobody can honor.

transition_in.carries_over: The two gift-card pools.
transition_in.introduces: The loyalty program not launched, for the same reason of separate systems.

sections.heading: The Choices
sections.controlling_idea: A merchant can run promotions in four ways, and the platform's built-in promotions are enough until one promotion must be the same rule in two systems the platform does not control.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the model into a decision: which arrangement fits, and why governance is the first improvement.

flow.rationale: Four parallel options from the least to the most machinery, with the non-design last, then the rule for choosing: the rule can be read only after the options it chooses between.

transition_in.carries_over: The promotion system and the stored-value ledgers as they must work.
transition_in.introduces: The four ways a merchant can obtain them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A merchant can run promotions in four ways, the fourth of which is common and not good.
The platform's built-in promotions come with documented combination rules and limits, and fit any merchant whose promotions fit the platform's vocabulary.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A promotion or loyalty app adds what the platform does not model and becomes a second writer of the price, with its own rules and failure modes.

transition_in.introduces: The third way: a separate engine every channel calls.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Rules hard-coded in a theme, a script or a marketplace listing are copies that drift, so nobody can say what the price was on a given day.

evidence.what: The four options compared on where the final discount is computed, order of evaluation and stop rule, the same promotion across channels, allocation to lines, stored value across channels, and which scale stages each fits.

sections.heading: In Practice
sections.controlling_idea: Law, abuse and measurement each ask the promotion system to record something, and Kestrel & Pine's plan for Black Friday 2027 shows the chapter's rules written down for one campaign.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies dated public evidence for the data a promotion system must keep, and shows the governance and allocation fixes in one plan.

flow.rationale: Three parallel public findings, then the one company plan that answers the incident the chapter opened with: the plan comes last because it uses the governance rule from the choices and the allocation from the system description.

transition_in.carries_over: The model and the choice of arrangement.
transition_in.introduces: Dated public examples of what promotions must record, and the plan Kestrel & Pine wrote after the incident.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three dated public sources show what the outside asks a promotion system to record (the law a price history, abuse a check of who the customer is, measurement a record of the offers made), and Kestrel & Pine's 2027 plan then shows the chapter's rules written down for one campaign.
The EU's prior-price rule turns a promotion into a data requirement: a price history per SKU and country that can give the lowest price of the last 30 days when a promotion is published.

evidence.what: Directive (EU) 2019/2161, applied from 28 May 2022; the Dutch regulator ACM supervising from 1 January 2023 with a worked example (€50 raised to €70 and cut 35% is a 9% discount); fines published 11 June 2024 against five named web shops; § 11 PAngV in Germany.
evidence.shows: The rule is enforced, so the price history is a legal requirement and not a nicety.
evidence.source: Directive (EU) 2019/2161; ACM publications of 6 December 2022 and 11 June 2024

evidence.what: Had the Price Drift run into November, the German strike-through price for the Ridgewalker would legally have been €179, not €199.
evidence.shows: The rule applied to the running example.

transition_in.carries_over: The three outside demands just named.
transition_in.introduces: The first: the EU's prior-price rule and the price history it requires.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Promotion abuse is an identity problem: its main forms, several accounts for one sign-up offer, self-referral and guessable codes, all exploit a weak check of who the customer is.

evidence.what: Ravelin's 2020 article names multi-accounting, self-referral and guessable codes; its figure that 53% of merchants saw more abuse is a vendor survey without a published sample.
evidence.shows: The taxonomy is usable; the figure is directional only.

transition_in.carries_over: A requirement the law places on promotion data.
transition_in.introduces: A requirement abuse places on it: knowing the customer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Whether a promotion earned anything can be measured only against a holdout group not given the offer, which requires the platform to record which promotions were offered.

evidence.what: Gubela, Lessmann and Jaroszewicz (2019): judge coupon campaigns on revenue uplift, not conversions; Gubela and Lessmann (2021): of several coupon types, only a €15 coupon produced positive incremental revenue.
evidence.shows: Redemption rate overstates effect, because many redeemers would have bought anyway.

transition_in.carries_over: What abuse requires the system to know.
transition_in.introduces: What measurement requires it to record.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For Black Friday 2027 Milan and Noor wrote the promotion plan as a table in which every row has an owner, an order of evaluation and a stop rule, stated the free-shipping threshold the way the cart computes it, and tested the plan against every active promotion in a staging copy.

evidence.what: Five rows (20% off outerwear, welcome code 10%, free shipping over €75, the store promotion, marketplace deals) with type, order, what each combines with, stop and owner, as the published chapter gave them: the outerwear discount stops further discounts, the welcome code never combines with it (the better one applies), and the shipping threshold is on the discounted subtotal and stated on the product page.
evidence.shows: Each of the three 2026 faults has a row or a column that prevents it.

transition_in.introduces: Kestrel & Pine's written plan for the next campaign.

evidence.what: Ruben Alves added the net line price to the integration contract under decision W5; neither change cost software.
evidence.shows: The fixes are ownership and a field in an export, not a new engine.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Promotions fail in six recurring ways, and each can be detected by comparing what was computed with what was recorded and recovered by correcting the record.

advances_thesis.how: Shows what breaks when a clause of the thesis is missing: an unowned stacking rule, two computations of one discount, a missing allocation, an unchecked balance.

flow.rationale: Six parallel failures, each the absence of something an earlier section established (an owned stop rule, one computation of the discount, a consistent code ledger, an idempotent stored-value debit, the allocation, a published end). The list opens with unintended stacking because it is the 2026 failure the plan just answered; no timeline is claimed, because round-3 readers found the list only partly follows a promotion's life.

transition_in.carries_over: The plan made in advance for 2027.
transition_in.introduces: What still goes wrong, how each failure is noticed and how it is repaired.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A written plan prevents the 2026 bug but does not stop promotions from going wrong; the failures that still happen follow, each with how to notice it and how to repair it.
Unintended stacking is detected by a daily report of orders with more than one discount and repaired by honoring the orders and fixing the setting.

transition_in.carries_over: The failures that still happen despite the plan.
transition_in.introduces: The first failure, when the campaign starts: unintended stacking.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The estimate and the final discount disagree when the page and the cart compute by different rules; logging both per session detects it.

transition_in.carries_over: Stacking, the first failure.
transition_in.introduces: A second: the page and the cart disagree.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Codes leak or are guessed, which shows as redemptions per code per hour above the expected rate.

transition_in.carries_over: Failures of the discount calculation in the cart.
transition_in.introduces: A failure at redemption: the code itself leaks or is guessed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stored value is debited twice, or not at all, when a checkout is retried or a payment message arrives late; ledger entries that reference the checkout attempt show the duplicate.

transition_in.carries_over: A failure of codes at checkout.
transition_in.introduces: A failure of the stored-value debit at the same moment.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The discount comes back twice when a return refunds the list price or a gift-card purchase is refunded both to the card and to the payment method; a weekly reconciliation of refunds against net line prices detects it.

transition_in.carries_over: Failures up to and at checkout.
transition_in.introduces: A failure after the order: the refund gives the discount back twice.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A promotion ends but a copy of it does not, on a cached page, a marketplace listing, a feed or a till; an end-of-promotion check on every channel detects it.

transition_in.carries_over: Failures during the promotion's life.
transition_in.introduces: A failure at its end: a copy outside the platform keeps running.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The stacking, the shipping charge and the over-refund looked like three faults and were one: each time, a number the customer or a later system relied on had been computed in one place and never recorded where the next reader looked. The same holds for stored value. A promotion system is therefore judged by what it writes down (the order and stop rule in the campaign, the net price on each line, the balance in a ledger) more than by how it computes.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant can prevent most promotion incidents without buying anything: give the combination settings an owner, test each campaign against the promotions already active, and make every order export carry the net price per line.

callback.to: The shopper who used a welcome code on a jacket and socks and returned the jacket.
callback.how: The reader can now compute the refund (the jacket's net line price) and say what had to be written to the order at checkout for the returns system to find it.

takeaway.content: Give the combination settings one owner, keep one promotion calendar with an order of evaluation per campaign, test every campaign against the active promotions, export the allocated net line price, and take the ten questions to the business.
